Published : Jul 28, 2026 16:34 IST - 6 MINS READ Ameer Shahul COMMents 0 GIFT THIS ARTICLE GIFT This is a premium feature available only to paid subscribers of Frontline Subscribe SHARE Copy link Email Facebook Twitter Telegram LinkedIn WhatsApp Reddit READ LATERSEE ALLRemove Collecting blood to test for dengue fever at a government hospital in New Delhi, a file picture. Dengue outbreaks are often reported across the country after the monsoon rains. | Photo Credit: MANISH SWARUP/AP India has crossed an important public health milestone in its battle against dengue. Nearly six decades after the country’s first recorded dengue epidemic, the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) on July 20 approved the QDENGA vaccine from Japan’s Takeda Pharmaceutical, making it the first dengue vaccine to receive marketing approval.The decision marks the beginning of a new chapter in the country’s battle against one of its fastest-growing infectious diseases. However, it should not be mistaken for the end of the story. If anything, it is the beginning of a much more complex process of who should receive the vaccine, how it should be deployed, and how the country can sustain its own scientific momentum in developing next-generation dengue vaccines.Dengue is unlike most viral diseases for which vaccines have been developed. The virus exists in four distinct serotypes, namely DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3, and DENV-4. Infection with one usually confers lifelong immunity only against that serotype. A subsequent infection with another serotype can trigger a far more severe illness through a phenomenon known as antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE). For vaccine developers, this has posed an extraordinary scientific challenge: producing a vaccine that offers balanced protection against all four serotypes without inadvertently increasing the risk of severe disease.The world’s first dengue vaccine, Dengvaxia, demonstrated just how difficult that challenge could be. Licenced in 2015 after years of research, it was initially hailed as a breakthrough. However, post-marketing studies revealed that individuals without prior dengue infection faced a higher risk of severe disease following vaccination.The fallout, particularly in the Philippines, where a nationwide immunisation programme had already begun, became one of the most controversial episodes in recent vaccine history. The episode not only reshaped WHO recommendations but also served as a cautionary reminder that scientific success must be matched by rigorous post-marketing surveillance and transparent communication.QDENGA represents a significant advance over first-generation dengue vaccines. Developed by Takeda, it can be administered without pre-vaccination screening for previous dengue infection and has demonstrated meaningful protection against symptomatic disease, hospitalisation, and severe dengue in large multinational clinical trials. Its approval by CDSCO, therefore, fills a long-standing gap in the country’s arsenal against dengue.However, a vaccine alone will not solve our dengue burden.Tens of thousands of laboratory-confirmed dengue cases are reported countrywide every year. But the actual number is believed to be many times higher because of under-reporting and limited surveillance. Climate change, changing rainfall patterns, rapid urbanisation, and expanding mosquito habitats are all lengthening transmission seasons and exposing new populations to infection. No vaccine, however effective, can substitute for sustained mosquito control, better urban planning, improved sanitation, and stronger disease surveillance.Questions about policyThe approval also raises important questions about vaccine policy. Should QDENGA be incorporated into Mission Indradhanush, the national immunisation programme? Should vaccination initially target high-incidence urban districts? Should it focus on children, healthcare workers, or populations with recurrent outbreaks? These are policy decisions that will require careful assessment of disease burden, cost-effectiveness and long-term epidemiological data.Equally important is what this development says about our vaccine ecosystem.Long before QDENGA arrived, Indian scientists had identified dengue as a national priority. National Institutes of Health of the US had licenced its experimental tetravalent dengue vaccine to several manufacturers, including Panacea Biotec, Serum Institute of India, Biological E. Ltd, and Indian Immunologicals. These partnerships enabled the Indian companies to build scientific capability while adapting vaccine platforms for local development. Serum Institute advanced its candidate into early clinical trials; Panacea Biotec established manufacturing processes with government support; and Indian Immunologicals continued to develop its own candidate under the National Biopharma Mission.Perhaps most significantly, scientists at the International Centre for Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology (ICGEB) in New Delhi pursued an entirely indigenous strategy. Their vaccine candidate, DSV-4, based on recombinant virus-like particles rather than live attenuated viruses, represents a distinctly Indian scientific innovation. Sun Pharma subsequently acquired the technology and is advancing it through clinical development.These efforts deserve as much attention as the approval of QDENGA itself.India’s vaccine story has often been told as one of manufacturing excellence. The country’s greatest achievement during the COVID-19 pandemic was producing vaccines at unprecedented scale. The next challenge is different: becoming a global leader not only in manufacturing but also in original vaccine discovery. Fogging operations in an Ahmedabad neighbourhood to combat dengue mosquito infestations, after heavy rainfall and waterlogging, on July 26, 2026. | Photo Credit: Hanif Sindhi/ANI The global dengue vaccine landscape is already evolving. Brazil’s Butantan Institute has reported encouraging results with a promising single-dose vaccine candidate, while researchers across the world are exploring mRNA platforms and next-generation technologies that may eventually provide broader and longer-lasting protection.Beyond dengueThe approval of QDENGA should also encourage India to broaden its ambitions beyond dengue. The same Aedes mosquito that transmits dengue is also responsible for spreading chikungunya and Zika, diseases whose geographic reach has expanded with climate change, urbanisation, and increasing human mobility.Chikungunya, once considered a self-limiting illness, is now recognised for causing prolonged and often debilitating joint pain that can persist for months or even years, imposing a substantial health and economic burden on affected communities. Despite recurrent outbreaks across India, there is still no licenced chikungunya vaccine in the country.Vaccine candidates based on virus-like particles and newer platforms have shown encouraging results in clinical trials, while the first chikungunya vaccines have begun receiving regulatory approvals in some countries. India, with its strong vaccine manufacturing capabilities and growing research ecosystem, is well positioned to participate in the next generation of vaccines against mosquito-borne diseases rather than merely serving as a manufacturing hub for products developed elsewhere.The approval of QDENGA is both an achievement and an opportunity. It offers hope to millions living under the constant threat of dengue, but it also reminds us that scientific progress is cumulative. Every imported technology should become the foundation for indigenous innovation. Every licencing agreement should strengthen domestic research capacity. Every successful vaccine should inspire the development of an even better one.The challenge before India is to build on the momentum and lead the development of vaccines not only against dengue but also against chikungunya, Zika, and the emerging arboviral threats of the future.Ameer Shahul is the author of best selling public health books Vaccine Nation and Heavy Metal. content_title: QDENGA Approval Marks New Phase in India’s Dengue Fight
content: India has crossed an important public health milestone in its battle against dengue . Nearly six decades after the country’s first recorded dengue epidemic, the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) on July 20 approved the QDENGA vaccine from Japan’s Takeda Pharmaceutical, making it the first dengue vaccine to receive marketing approval. The decision marks the beginning of a new chapter in the country’s battle against one of its fastest-growing infectious diseases. However, it should not be mistaken for the end of the story. If anything, it is the beginning of a much more complex process of who should receive the vaccine, how it should be deployed, and how the country can sustain its own scientific momentum in developing next-generation dengue vaccines. Dengue is unlike most viral diseases for which vaccines have been developed. The virus exists in four distinct serotypes, namely DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3, and DENV-4. Infection with one usually confers lifelong immunity only against that serotype. A subsequent infection with another serotype can trigger a far more severe illness through a phenomenon known as antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE). For vaccine developers, this has posed an extraordinary scientific challenge: producing a vaccine that offers balanced protection against all four serotypes without inadvertently increasing the risk of severe disease. The world’s first dengue vaccine, Dengvaxia, demonstrated just how difficult that challenge could be. Licenced in 2015 after years of research, it was initially hailed as a breakthrough. However, post-marketing studies revealed that individuals without prior dengue infection faced a higher risk of severe disease following vaccination. The fallout, particularly in the Philippines, where a nationwide immunisation programme had already begun, became one of the most controversial episodes in recent vaccine history. The episode not only reshaped WHO recommendations but also served as a cautionary reminder that scientific success must be matched by rigorous post-marketing surveillance and transparent communication. QDENGA represents a significant advance over first-generation dengue vaccines. Developed by Takeda, it can be administered without pre-vaccination screening for previous dengue infection and has demonstrated meaningful protection against symptomatic disease, hospitalisation, and severe dengue in large multinational clinical trials. Its approval by CDSCO, therefore, fills a long-standing gap in the country’s arsenal against dengue. However, a vaccine alone will not solve our dengue burden. Tens of thousands of laboratory-confirmed dengue cases are reported countrywide every year. But the actual number is believed to be many times higher because of under-reporting and limited surveillance. Climate change, changing rainfall patterns, rapid urbanisation, and expanding mosquito habitats are all lengthening transmission seasons and exposing new populations to infection. No vaccine, however effective, can substitute for sustained mosquito control, better urban planning, improved sanitation, and stronger disease surveillance. Questions about policy The approval also raises important questions about vaccine policy. Should QDENGA be incorporated into Mission Indradhanush, the national immunisation programme? Should vaccination initially target high-incidence urban districts? Should it focus on children, healthcare workers, or populations with recurrent outbreaks? These are policy decisions that will require careful assessment of disease burden, cost-effectiveness and long-term epidemiological data. Equally important is what this development says about our vaccine ecosystem. Long before QDENGA arrived, Indian scientists had identified dengue as a national priority. National Institutes of Health of the US had licenced its experimental tetravalent dengue vaccine to several manufacturers, including Panacea Biotec, Serum Institute of India, Biological E. Ltd, and Indian Immunologicals. These partnerships enabled the Indian companies to build scientific capability while adapting vaccine platforms for local development. Serum Institute advanced its candidate into early clinical trials; Panacea Biotec established manufacturing processes with government support; and Indian Immunologicals continued to develop its own candidate under the National Biopharma Mission. Perhaps most significantly, scientists at the International Centre for Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology (ICGEB) in New Delhi pursued an entirely indigenous strategy. Their vaccine candidate, DSV-4, based on recombinant virus-like particles rather than live attenuated viruses, represents a distinctly Indian scientific innovation. Sun Pharma subsequently acquired the technology and is advancing it through clinical development. These efforts deserve as much attention as the approval of QDENGA itself. India’s vaccine story has often been told as one of manufacturing excellence. The country’s greatest achievement during the COVID-19 pandemic was producing vaccines at unprecedented scale. The next challenge is different: becoming a global leader not only in manufacturing but also in original vaccine discovery. Fogging operations in an Ahmedabad neighbourhood to combat dengue mosquito infestations, after heavy rainfall and waterlogging, on July 26, 2026. | Photo Credit: Hanif Sindhi/ANI The global dengue vaccine landscape is already evolving. Brazil’s Butantan Institute has reported encouraging results with a promising single-dose vaccine candidate, while researchers across the world are exploring mRNA platforms and next-generation technologies that may eventually provide broader and longer-lasting protection. Beyond dengue The approval of QDENGA should also encourage India to broaden its ambitions beyond dengue. The same Aedes mosquito that transmits dengue is also responsible for spreading chikungunya and Zika, diseases whose geographic reach has expanded with climate change, urbanisation, and increasing human mobility. Chikungunya, once considered a self-limiting illness, is now recognised for causing prolonged and often debilitating joint pain that can persist for months or even years, imposing a substantial health and economic burden on affected communities. Despite recurrent outbreaks across India, there is still no licenced chikungunya vaccine in the country. Vaccine candidates based on virus-like particles and newer platforms have shown encouraging results in clinical trials, while the first chikungunya vaccines have begun receiving regulatory approvals in some countries. India, with its strong vaccine manufacturing capabilities and growing research ecosystem, is well positioned to participate in the next generation of vaccines against mosquito-borne diseases rather than merely serving as a manufacturing hub for products developed elsewhere. The approval of QDENGA is both an achievement and an opportunity. It offers hope to millions living under the constant threat of dengue, but it also reminds us that scientific progress is cumulative. Every imported technology should become the foundation for indigenous innovation. Every licencing agreement should strengthen domestic research capacity. Every successful vaccine should inspire the development of an even better one. The challenge before India is to build on the momentum and lead the development of vaccines not only against dengue but also against chikungunya, Zika, and the emerging arboviral threats of the future. Across many Indian homes, a fever often starts the same way: a slight chill, tiredness, body pain, and the hope that a couple of days of rest will solve everything. Sometimes it does.But sometimes, what looks like an ordinary viral fever turns out to be dengue, a disease that can worsen quickly if ignored.The challenge is that dengue does not always announce itself dramatically. In the first few days, it can closely resemble many other viral infections. That is why doctors say guessing at home or relying on internet advice can delay the right treatment.2/7Dengue is not just another viral feverMany people use the phrase "viral fever" for almost every fever that lasts a few days. Medically, however, viral fever is not a single disease.Dr Shilpa Rajendran, Chief of Medical Services & Consultant Intensivist, Even Healthcare, explained, "Dengue is a specific viral infection caused by the dengue virus and spread through the bite of infected Aedes mosquitoes. The infection can range from having no symptoms at all to causing a mild fever, or in some cases, severe complications such as dengue shock syndrome."She further said, "Viral fever, on the other hand, is a general term used for any fever caused by a virus, such as influenza, COVID-19, or chickenpox."That distinction matters because the cause, the possible complications, and even the monitoring required can be completely different.While most viral fevers improve with rest, fluids, and time, dengue requires careful observation because some patients can deteriorate after the fever begins to settle. 3/7Why the symptoms can fool almost anyoneOne of the biggest reasons dengue gets missed is because its early symptoms overlap with several common viral illnesses.A person may develop:Sudden high feverHeadacheFatigueMuscle achesLoss of appetite​These symptoms alone cannot confirm whether someone has dengue or another viral infection.However, dengue often begins to show certain clues that doctors pay close attention to.Dr Rajendran said, "While dengue and other viral fevers can have similar symptoms, dengue often stands out because of severe body aches, intense joint, bone pain and retro orbital pain and a rapid drop in platelet count. Doctors also use blood tests such as the NS1 antigen test and IgM/IgG antibody tests to confirm a dengue infection."Pain behind the eyes, often called retro-orbital pain, is one symptom that is more commonly associated with dengue than with routine viral fevers. Many patients also describe feeling as though every muscle and bone aches, which is why dengue has historically been nicknamed "breakbone fever."Still, doctors caution against trying to diagnose dengue based only on symptoms because many illnesses can overlap.4/7Why getting the diagnosis right changes everythingPerhaps the biggest misconception is that platelet count alone decides whether someone has dengue. Doctors say this is only one part of the picture.A confirmed diagnosis helps healthcare teams monitor the patient's hydration status, blood counts, warning signs, and overall clinical condition at the right time.5/7The days when fever comes down can actually be the most importantMany families assume that once the fever disappears, recovery has begun. With dengue, that assumption can sometimes be dangerous.The WHO explains that the critical phase often begins around the time the fever settles, usually after several days of illness. During this period, some patients may develop warning signs that require urgent medical attention.6/7What should you do if you develop a fever during dengue season?There is no need to panic every time a fever appears. But there is every reason to be careful. While waiting for medical advice:​Drink adequate fluids unless advised otherwise by your doctor.Rest as much as possible.Do not self-medicate without medical guidance.Watch carefully for any warning signs, especially if the fever begins to settle.If your doctor recommends blood tests, get them done at the advised time rather than too early or too late.Finally, prevention remains the strongest defence. Since dengue spreads through Aedes mosquitoes, removing stagnant water around homes, using mosquito repellents, wearing full-sleeved clothing, and keeping windows protected with screens can significantly reduce the risk of infection.A fever may look ordinary on day one. content_title: Tropical Diseases Like Dengue Fever and Chikungunya Are on the Rise in Europe
content: In September 2024, a handful of patients showed up at the emergency room in the coastal city of Fano, Italy, with mysterious symptoms: a rash on their hands and feet, fever, nausea, and diarrhea. Doctors sent for various tests until one came back with a positive result for dengue, a viral infection spread by mosquitoes, usually in tropical regions of the world. They tested the other patients, and, sure enough, they had dengue too. The strange thing? None of the patients had recently traveled to a country where they might expect to pick up a dengue infection. The only thing they had in common was visiting a particular neighbourhood in Fano. As climate change increases temperatures across Europe, invasive mosquitoes are spreading and introducing disease agents that Europeans would usually think about only when traveling to other continents. The Fano outbreak wasn’t the first time dengue had been detected as spreading locally in mainland Europe, but it was significantly larger than previous incidents, with 199 cases detected between mid-August and mid-October of 2024. Over the past few years, European countries have reported outbreaks of other mosquito-borne viruses such as chikungunya, a painful disease that causes joint swelling, and West Nile virus. In a heating world, so-called tropical diseases are no longer restricted to tropical regions—and researchers expect the trend to continue. The main current culprit is the mosquito Aedes albopictus, commonly known as the Asian tiger mosquito (or just the tiger mosquito, given it’s now found across all continents). Unlike many mosquito species, it bites in the daytime as well as at night. The tiger mosquito already has established populations across Europe, particularly in the south, and we can expect it to move north, says Riccardo Moretti, a senior researcher at the Italian National Agency for New Technologies, Energy and Sustainable Economic Development (ENEA), who has been working on tiger mosquitos for more than 20 years. The tiger mosquito thrives between 20 and 30 degrees Celsius (68 to 86 Fahrenheit), but it can still live at around 10 Celsius (50 Fahrenheit). “This means that at the moment there are already conditions that could allow for the spread of the Asian tiger mosquito, even in England,” Moretti says. At the moment, these conditions are limited to the warmest part of the year in northern European countries. But farther south, such as in Greece, the mosquito season is elongating. Moretti says researchers have found adults buzzing around until December and reappearing already in March; they overwinter as eggs. “There is a concrete risk that in the next few years, we could have a population capable of surviving throughout the year,” Moretti says. At the moment, cases of mosquito-borne diseases in Europe tend to occur toward the end of summer. This is when tiger mosquitoes are most prevalent, and it’s also when more people return from travel. Someone unwittingly brings back an infection that isn’t found in Europe—dengue, say—and gets bitten by a tiger mosquito. The mosquito goes on to bite other people, and the disease spreads locally. But as the weather cools, the mosquitoes get less active and cases subside. If the mosquito season lasts longer, however, more infections can occur. Ultimately, says Moretti, there’s a risk that tropical diseases like dengue could become endemic in parts of Europe, meaning the disease is always there. “It is completely different dealing with occasional cases of virus transmission, and instead dealing with a permanent status of possibility of transmission,” he says. A difference of a couple of degrees can make a big difference. Earlier this year, a study found that the conditions required for tiger mosquitoes to transmit chikungunya were cooler than previously thought. The mosquitoes can spread the virus at just 14 degrees Celsius (57 degrees Fahrenheit) rather than 16 (61 degrees Fahrenheit), meaning outbreaks could occur in most European countries and for longer periods. “That difference of two degrees matters a lot when we are talking about global warming,” says Sandeep Tegar, an epidemiological modeler at the UK Centre for Ecology and Hydrology, who led the study. While warmer temperatures may generally create better conditions for mosquitoes, this isn’t the full story. Too hot—more than 35 degrees Celsius (95 degrees Fahrenheit)—and tiger mosquitoes struggle to survive. Southern France and Spain, impacted by recent heat waves and wildfires, may actually have fewer mosquitoes this year, says Frederic Bartumeus, an ecologist at the Spanish scientific research center CEAB: “It’s not been a great mosquito season in these areas, because it’s too hot and it’s too dry.” Rain is important, as mosquitoes need standing water to breed: This is where they lay their eggs, and where the larvae and pupae develop. “If it rains too little, then there’s not sufficient breeding sites,” explains Felipe Colón González, technology lead and expert in climate and infectious diseases at the UK-based health foundation Wellcome. “But if it rains too much, then it can wash away the mosquito breeding sites.” Humidity also plays a role. Beyond mosquitoes, climate conditions can have different effects on the viruses they carry, and on the behavior of humans—an important consideration in the spread of disease. This all makes modeling patterns of mosquitoes and the diseases they spread more complex, so ongoing surveillance is critical. It may be possible to reduce mosquito populations if they’re caught early enough. ENEA’s Moretti is part of a team that recently ran an experiment to control a tiger mosquito population in Italy by releasing more than a million male mosquitoes that were reproductively incompatible—meaning when they mate, the female lays sterile eggs. This significantly reduced the number of fertile mosquito eggs in the area. But breeding mosquitoes in a specialized biofactory was expensive. In this case, the mosquitoes were bred in Miami by Google’s Debug program and shipped to Italy. In any case, it would be impossible to eliminate mosquitoes, Moretti says—they’re too efficient at colonizing new areas. “But what is important is to drastically reduce the risks of transmissions of tropical viruses.” Colón González says the main test for European countries is whether public health systems can keep isolated outbreaks from becoming major crises. “A common misconception is that preparedness is mainly about predicting disease outbreaks,” he says. “In reality, preparedness is about building the system that allows the public health infrastructure to effectively react when the risks emerge.” In this regard, Europe has an advantage over some parts of the world: Reliable public health and information systems mean that, so far, cases of mosquito-transmitted diseases have remained lower than in other areas of the world with a similar climate. As invasive mosquitoes continue to settle across the Continent, Europeans may have to get used to taking the kinds of precautions that people in tropical regions are accustomed to. In Spain, Bartumeus already has mosquito nets on his windows and regularly empties standing water, such as that left sitting in flower pots. He uses mosquito repellant and wears long trousers if he’s going to be outside in the evening. “Simple things like that, that’s the only thing you can do,” he says. Soon, the tiger mosquito may have company. Another invasive species, Aedes aegypti, or the yellow fever mosquito, has already established populations in Cyprus and the Portuguese archipelago of Madeira. As its name would suggest, it can transmit yellow fever, but it also carries dengue, chikungunya, and Zika. Yellow fever mosquitoes can’t tolerate temperatures quite as cool as the tiger mosquito can, but it has been detected making occasional jaunts north, likely transported on cargo. Its most recent destination: a service station in Luxembourg

content: The Florida Department of Health recorded the first case of dengue acquired locally in Hillsborough County this summer. Dengue fever is a mosquito-borne disease transmitted through the bite of the mosquito species aedes aegypti and aedes albopictus, which are both found in Florida. Most cases of dengue in the U.S. occur in travelers infected in areas with risk , like the Caribbean and Central and South America. In Florida, local spread is common. Typical symptoms of dengue include fever, severe headache, eye pain, muscle, joint and bone pain, bleeding, nausea, vomiting and rash, according to the health department. The joint and bone pain that some people experience gives dengue its second name, bone-break fever. Symptoms typically last 2-7 days and develop within two weeks of an infected mosquito bite. If symptoms of dengue develop, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention advise seeing a healthcare provider. There is no specific medicine to treat dengue — just rest, drinking fluids and easing symptoms with pain relief. Forty-two cases of dengue have been recorded in Florida so far this year, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The center reported 506 cases in Florida last year. Miami-Dade County accounted for over 60% of the state’s cases last year. Compared to Miami-Dade’s 316 cases, Hillsborough County recorded 28 and Pinellas County had eight in 2025. Hillsborough reported seven locally acquired dengue cases between July 2024 and January 2025. The health department and Hillsborough County Mosquito Control coordinated aerial spraying as a prevention effort. Florida is currently in the middle of mosquito season, which runs from March to October. To help prevent mosquito bites, the health department encourages residents to drain water from outside areas to reduce where mosquitoes can breed and lay eggs, cover themselves with protective clothing while outdoors and keep doors and windows closed. The department also recommends applying insect repellent that contains DEET (10-30%), picaridin, oil of lemon eucalyptus, para-menthane-diol, 2-undecanone or IR3535. For children under two months old, the department recommends mosquito netting for protection. Residents should report dead birds to the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission’s website , according to the department. The Florida Department of Health regularly conducts statewide surveillance for mosquito-borne illnesses, including dengue, West Nile virus infections, Eastern equine encephalitis, St. Louis encephalitis, malaria and chikungunya

complications beginDengue can look like a simple viral fever at first: Doctor reveals the warning signs that help tell the difference before complications beginAadya Jha / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Jul 27, 2026, 14:07 ISTShareAA+Text SizeSmallMediumLargeFollow us 1/7Dengue and viral fever often begin with similar symptomsMonsoon brings relief from the heat, but it also marks the return of mosquito-borne illnesses. Across many Indian homes, a fever often starts the same way: a slight chill, tiredness, body pain, and the hope that a couple of days of rest will solve everything. Sometimes it does.But sometimes, what looks like an ordinary viral fever turns out to be dengue, a disease that can worsen quickly if ignored.The challenge is that dengue does not always announce itself dramatically. In the first few days, it can closely resemble many other viral infections. That is why doctors say guessing at home or relying on internet advice can delay the right treatment.Read More2/7Dengue is not just another viral feverMany people use the phrase "viral fever" for almost every fever that lasts a few days. Medically, however, viral fever is not a single disease.Dr Shilpa Rajendran, Chief of Medical Services & Consultant Intensivist, Even Healthcare, explained, "Dengue is a specific viral infection caused by the dengue virus and spread through the bite of infected Aedes mosquitoes. The infection can range from having no symptoms at all to causing a mild fever, or in some cases, severe complications such as dengue shock syndrome."She further said, "Viral fever, on the other hand, is a general term used for any fever caused by a virus, such as influenza, COVID-19, or chickenpox."That distinction matters because the cause, the possible complications, and even the monitoring required can be completely different.While most viral fevers improve with rest, fluids, and time, dengue requires careful observation because some patients can deteriorate after the fever begins to settle. Read More3/7Why the symptoms can fool almost anyoneOne of the biggest reasons dengue gets missed is because its early symptoms overlap with several common viral illnesses.A person may develop:Sudden high feverHeadacheFatigueMuscle achesLoss of appetite​These symptoms alone cannot confirm whether someone has dengue or another viral infection.However, dengue often begins to show certain clues that doctors pay close attention to.Dr Rajendran said, "While dengue and other viral fevers can have similar symptoms, dengue often stands out because of severe body aches, intense joint, bone pain and retro orbital pain and a rapid drop in platelet count. Doctors also use blood tests such as the NS1 antigen test and IgM/IgG antibody tests to confirm a dengue infection."Pain behind the eyes, often called retro-orbital pain, is one symptom that is more commonly associated with dengue than with routine viral fevers. Many patients also describe feeling as though every muscle and bone aches, which is why dengue has historically been nicknamed "breakbone fever."Still, doctors caution against trying to diagnose dengue based only on symptoms because many illnesses can overlap.Read More4/7Why getting the diagnosis right changes everythingPerhaps the biggest misconception is that platelet count alone decides whether someone has dengue. Doctors say this is only one part of the picture.A confirmed diagnosis helps healthcare teams monitor the patient's hydration status, blood counts, warning signs, and overall clinical condition at the right time.5/7The days when fever comes down can actually be the most importantMany families assume that once the fever disappears, recovery has begun. With dengue, that assumption can sometimes be dangerous.The WHO explains that the critical phase often begins around the time the fever settles, usually after several days of illness. During this period, some patients may develop warning signs that require urgent medical attention.Read More6/7What should you do if you develop a fever during dengue season?There is no need to panic every time a fever appears. But there is every reason to be careful. While waiting for medical advice:​Drink adequate fluids unless advised otherwise by your doctor.Rest as much as possible.Do not self-medicate without medical guidance.Watch carefully for any warning signs, especially if the fever begins to settle.If your doctor recommends blood tests, get them done at the advised time rather than too early or too late.Finally, prevention remains the strongest defence. Since dengue spreads through Aedes mosquitoes, removing stagnant water around homes, using mosquito repellents, wearing full-sleeved clothing, and keeping windows protected with screens can significantly reduce the risk of infection.A fever may look ordinary on day one. But paying attention to the small differences, seeking medical advice early, and avoiding assumptions can make all the difference when dengue is circulating in the community.Read More7/7Medical experts consultedThis article includes expert inputs shared with TOI Health by:Dr Shilpa Rajendran, Chief of Medical Services & Consultant Intensivist, Even Healthcare.Inputs were used to explain how dengue differs from a common viral fever, why recognising the difference early is important, and when medical evaluation should not be delayed.Read MoreFollow Us On Social MediaPhotostoriesYou've crossed it countless times, but do you know why it's called a zebra crossing?'Avengers: Doomsday': What details did fans miss in the trailer?
